{"id": "26:11/q04", "question": "Why are these people called wrongdoers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q04/p1", "position": "They combined disbelief and idolatry with oppression of the Israelites and others.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes disbelief; Abū Ḥayyān and Kur'an Yolu mention enslavement and the killing of sons, the latter also denial of God's existence and oneness. Al-Biqāʿī says they wronged themselves, Israelites, and other servants. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes associationism against oneself from violating others' rights, citing 2:114 and 6:82 for the Qur'anic range of ẓulm; he says the description makes their notorious oppression a reason for Moses's mission. Iṣlāḥī describes escalating rebellion without fear of wrath."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q05", "question": "What does al-Suddī report about Pharaoh's pursuit of Moses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q05/p1", "position": "Pharaoh pursued Moses with Haman leading an army of 1.7 million horses, none female.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits the report from al-Suddī."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q06", "question": "How is the verb in 'أَلَا يَتَّقُونَ' read?", "turns_on": "Whether the commissioned speech describes absent people, turns to address them, or preserves a first-person object or address in the final vowel.", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q06/p1", "position": "The common reading has third-person yāʾ: 'will they not fear?'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls it narration before direct address; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī say the people are absent from the immediate address. Al-Farrāʾ compares the alternation at 3:12. Al-Ṭabrisī glosses it as 'Is it not time for them to fear?' Al-Samīn notes an open final nūn and an omitted object, punishment; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ calls it rebuke from afar to be conveyed by Moses."}, {"id": "26:11/q06/p2", "position": "A tāʾ reading directly addresses Pharaoh's people: 'will you not fear?'", "reasons": "Readers named across the notes include ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Abū Ḥāzim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Yasār, Ḥammād ibn Salama, Shaqīq ibn Salama, and Abū Qilāba. Al-Ṭabrisī calls it noncanonical. Ibn Jinnī supplies 'say to them,' comparing 13:23–24; al-Naḥḥās and al-Farrāʾ compare 3:12. Al-Zamakhsharī describes a sudden accusatory turn to the absent culprits, made present through Moses's delivery; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say it heightens rebuke and reflection."}, {"id": "26:11/q06/p3", "position": "A reading has a kasra on the final nūn; one report also allows fatḥa.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī report the kasra; Abū Ḥayyān reports fatḥa or kasra; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī report kasra. Their competing parses are treated separately below."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q07", "question": "How is the reading with kasra on the nūn parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the vowel preserves an elided first-person object or results from a compressed vocative and imperative.", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q07/p1", "position": "It means 'will they not fear Me?' with the first-person object yāʾ elided.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī describes loss of one of two adjacent nūns and then the yāʾ, leaving its kasra. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Samīn also allow the retained kasra to stand for the object. Abū Ḥayyān reports an underlying 'will they not fear Me?' and explains elision by adjacent sukūns; al-Ālūsī derives the form from tattaqūnanī."}, {"id": "26:11/q07/p2", "position": "It is a vocative plus imperative: 'O people, fear Me.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī compares the address at 2:34 and the form at 27:25; the proposed derivation loses the alif of yāʾ in speech and writing. Al-Bayḍāwī mentions the parallel 'alā yā usjudū'. Al-Samīn calls the parse remote; Abū Ḥayyān calls it far-fetched; al-Ālūsī says dropping both alifs is irregular."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q08", "question": "What does fearing God mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether taqwā is glossed as worship, reverence of God, or protective caution expressed through obedience and faith.", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q08/p1", "position": "To guard against God’s punishment and the consequences of wrongdoing through obedience, faith, and good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī say obedience averts punishment; al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz adds belief. Al-Ṭabrisī derives taqwā from making a protective barrier by doing good and avoiding blameworthy things; Ibn al-Jawzī describes taking protective precautions. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives fear and caution with an implicit object, the consequences of injustice, comparing 8:56. Study Quran's reported view includes mindfulness of the Hereafter's punishment. Al-Qāshānī evokes God's overwhelming force and annihilating wrath; al-Burūsawī combines faith, obedience, and averting punishment."}, {"id": "26:11/q08/p2", "position": "To worship God.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses the question as asking whether they will worship God. Al-Dāmaghānī says ittaqū can bear 'worship,' citing 16:2 and 16:51."}, {"id": "26:11/q08/p3", "position": "To become reverent or mindful of God.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām describes the mission as calling them to fear God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the phrase both denies present reverence and orders it; Study Quran reports both the question of reverence and, depending on vocalization, reverencing God. Al-Ālūsī says Moses speaks for God as at 2:186, so it can mean 'fear Me'."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q09", "question": "How is taqwā distinguished from faith and waraʿ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q09/p1", "position": "Taqwā is protective precaution; unlike faith it is unmixed, and unlike waraʿ it is not limited to uncertain matters.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī's teacher ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh calls taqwā more commendable than faith because faith may be mixed with other things. Ibn al-Jawzī defines waraʿ as avoiding a doubtful matter whose cause is conjectural and restraining oneself from uncertain consequences."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q10", "question": "What is the force of 'أَلَا' in the question?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is one exhortative particle, interrogation plus negation, or an attention marker.", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q10/p1", "position": "It is an exhortative particle urging the people to become God-fearing.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Burūsawī and al-Ālūsī take this as the apparent force; al-Ālūsī extends it to every reading. Al-Itqān distinguishes insistent exhortation from gentler invitation, both requesting action with verbs, citing 2:44, 26:11, 37:91 and 24:22. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it one particle of urging and makes the clause an explanation of 'go'. Al-Nasafī says it is time for them to fear; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it commands reverence while denying its presence."}, {"id": "26:11/q10/p2", "position": "It is interrogative hamza plus negative lā, denying that they fear God and expressing astonishment.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says the combination asserts the negative proposition. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the interrogative as rejecting their absence of fear and registering Moses's astonishment. Al-Zamakhsharī's analysis, reported by al-Samīn, also treats it as a denial; Asad reports al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī reading it as the factual assertion that they refuse God-consciousness."}, {"id": "26:11/q10/p3", "position": "It is an attention particle.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn mentions this as another grammatical view; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it in favor of exhortation."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q11", "question": "How does 'أَلَا يَتَّقُونَ' attach to Moses's commission?", "turns_on": "Whether the question is independent, implied speech to be delivered, or a circumstance modifying the wrongdoers; the last parse faces two stated syntactic objections.", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q11/p1", "position": "It is a fresh, independent question after the command to go.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim recommends stopping after 'Pharaoh's people' because the meaning is complete. Al-Zamakhsharī sees a fresh divine remark registering extreme wrongdoing and amazement at confidence despite God's punishment; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Burūsawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr similarly make it a separate question. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it prepares Moses for entrenched resistance known from his upbringing."}, {"id": "26:11/q11/p2", "position": "It is speech for Moses to convey, with an implied 'tell them' or 'saying'.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Jinnī supply 'tell them'; Ibn Jinnī compares the implied 'they say' at 13:23–24. Al-Ṭabrisī gives this for the tāʾ reading; al-Ālūsī makes the phrase circumstantial with an implied speech verb. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the exhortation as explaining 'go' and says the command can be reported by meaning, as in 5:117; he points to the later explicit command to go and speak at 26:16."}, {"id": "26:11/q11/p3", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause: they are wrongdoers while not fearing God.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn attach the circumstance to the pronoun in 'the wrongdoers'. Abū Ḥayyān objects that 'Pharaoh's people' intervenes between governor and dependent and that material before interrogative hamza cannot govern what follows; al-Samīn records the Shaykh's same objections. Al-Ālūsī finds a reply that the intervening phrase is not foreign unconvincing."}]}
{"id": "26:11/q12", "question": "What does the question convey about Pharaoh's people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:11/q12/p1", "position": "It rebukes their established lack of piety and calls them toward it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the question implies they do not fear God and that Moses must call them to piety. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī describe amazement at their injustice and audacity. Al-Biqāʿī hears anger over growing stubbornness during long respite; Iṣlāḥī hears anger, yearning, rebuke and nearness of punishment. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ calls the third-person wording a rebuke from afar. Asad reports al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī taking it as a factual assertion of refusal."}]}

{"id": "26:18/q01", "question": "What happened before Pharaoh gave this reply?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over whether the audience followed a year's wait or a nighttime arrival; the commentators also identify speech omitted by the condensed narrative.", "positions": [{"id": "26:18/q01/p1", "position": "Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and delivered their message; the narrative leaves their arrival and speech implicit.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says they delivered the message; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān identify the omitted words as their going and speaking, supplied by context; Iṣlāḥī adds the courtiers, warning, and demand to release the Israelites."}, {"id": "26:18/q01/p2", "position": "Moses and Aaron waited a year at Pharaoh's gate before he admitted them to mock their claim.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says Pharaoh initially withheld access; Qatāda, as cited by Bursawī, says he recognized Moses after hearing the message; al-Ālūsī adds the porter's announcement of a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. {"id": "26:18/q03", "question": "What is Pharaoh trying to do with the question about raising Moses?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over whether Pharaoh's primary aim was to claim gratitude, belittle Moses, challenge the mission, establish identity, or expose a moral defect; several commentators combine aims.", "positions": [{"id": "26:18/q03/p1", "position": "He claims a favor and demands gratitude for raising Moses.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports the favor reading; al-Ṭabrisī says Pharaoh claims credit for kindness; Ibn al-Jawzī and Ibn Kathīr connect the claim to Moses' later killing of an Egyptian, which Pharaoh calls repayment for housing, feeding, and protecting him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī ask when Moses acquired the claimed mission."}, {"id": "26:18/q03/p4", "position": "He asks whether Moses really is the same person formerly raised there.", "reasons": "Jishumī records this as a further possibility, consistent with his account of Pharaoh asking if Moses was the child they raised."}, {"id": "26:18/q03/p5", "position": "His recital of favors exposes a lack of chivalry.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī says a benefactor should not lord favors over someone; al-Ṭabrisī reports the alternative that Pharaoh disclosed his meanness by recounting them."}]}

{"id": "26:18/q11", "question": "How do Arabic oath and fixed source expressions involving عُمُر work?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish an oath by life from an accusative source formula with an understood verb; the other fixed formulas are grammatical analogies.", "positions": [{"id": "26:18/q11/p1", "position": "The oath expressions swear by life; in an oath the initial vowel is open and the mīm still.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba glosses laʿamruka and wa-laʿamr Allāh as oaths by your or God's life. Al-Zajjāj reports Sībawayh, al-Khalīl, and the Basrans restricting the oath form to laʿamr Allāh; Jishumī states its voweling, and al-Naḥḥās reports Sībawayh's explanation that fatḥa eases pronunciation."}, {"id": "26:18/q11/p2", "position": "ʿAmraka Allāh is an accusative fixed source expression standing for an omitted verb; similar expressions clarify its syntax.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says fixed maṣdars occupy one slot and lack ordinary article, nominative, and genitive uses, unlike free sources; ʿamraka Allāh and qaʿdaka Allāh are analogous to nashadtuka Allāh. Al-Khalīl says the proposed verb ʿammartuka is explanatory, not necessarily spoken; an unnamed poet and Ibn Aḥmar attest it. Sībawayh compares subḥān Allāh, with its omitted verb and definiteness from use (though Umayya's verse has tanwīn), and rayḥānah, meaning provision; Abū al-Khaṭṭāb glosses subḥān as God's freedom from evil, supported by al-Aʿshā's disavowal line. Ghufrānaka lā kufrānaka seeks forgiveness, not disbelief. Salāman can mean separation, as Abū al-Khaṭṭāb explains Abū Rabīʿa's wording; Umayya's poetry and some Arabs' raised salām bi-salām support the expression. Subbūḥan quddūsan are names with implied adhkuru; some Arabs raise them too. Khayr mā rudda fī ahl wa-māl patterns like khayr maqdam. Exclamatory karaman wa-ṣalafan omits a verb; Abū Murhab's karaman wa-ṭūl anf illustrates this."}]}

{"id": "26:18/q14", "question": "How many years did Moses live among Pharaoh's people?", "turns_on": "The transmitted chronologies give different lengths of residence or ages at departure: eighteen, thirty, forty, ten, and twelve.", "positions": [{"id": "26:18/q14/p1", "position": "Thirty years.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī's reports from Muqātil, al-Baghawī, Jishumī's unnamed report, al-Ṭabrisī's attribution to Mujāhid under a Muqātil speaker label, Ibn al-Jawzī's Muqātil report, and later chronologies all give thirty; al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz states it directly."}, {"id": "26:18/q14/p2", "position": "Eighteen years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this figure in al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, and Ibn al-Jawzī; al-Wāḥidī repeats the estimate alongside the gloss of walīd."}, {"id": "26:18/q14/p3", "position": "Forty years, or approximately forty.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī gives forty in al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī; Ibn al-Jawzī names Ibn al-Sāʾib; Ibn ʿĀshūr says about forty, supported in his account by Moses leaving at about forty after the killing."}, {"id": "26:18/q14/p4", "position": "He left at ten years of age.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this within a chronology that also says he was kept from entry for a year, returned at thirty, and lived fifty years after Pharaoh drowned."}, {"id": "26:18/q14/p5", "position": "He fled at twelve years of age.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this in a different chronology, after Moses struck the Egyptian."}]}
